clinicalPearls: A mosaic form of neurofibromatosis type 1 in which café-au-lait macules, freckling and/or neurofibromas are confined to one or a few body segments, often respecting the midline.
It results from a post-zygotic somatic NF1 mutation, so features are limited to the clonal cutaneous territory rather than being generalised.
Lesions frequently follow a broad dermatomal or Blaschkoid distribution and stop abruptly at the midline.
Most patients have no family history, but gonadal (germline) mosaicism means offspring can rarely inherit generalised NF1.
Systemic complications such as optic glioma and skeletal dysplasia are uncommon, though they can occur if deeper tissues carry the mutation.
Diagnosis is largely clinical; skin biopsy of a neurofibroma confirms the lesion type and mosaic NF1 can be demonstrated on lesional (not blood) tissue.
New or rapidly enlarging, painful nodules within the affected segment warrant assessment for malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour.
Genetic counselling should address the small but real reproductive risk from possible germline involvement.
reference.pathophysiology: Segmental neurofibromatosis is caused by a somatic loss-of-function mutation in the NF1 tumour-suppressor gene occurring after fertilisation, during embryonic development. Because the mutation arises in a single progenitor cell and is propagated only to its clonal descendants, neurofibromin deficiency is restricted to a delimited region of skin and sometimes underlying tissue, producing the characteristic segmental, midline-respecting distribution of café-au-lait macules, freckling and neurofibromas. Loss of neurofibromin removes negative regulation of Ras signalling within the affected clone, promoting the same Schwann-cell and melanocytic proliferations seen in generalised NF1 but confined to the mosaic territory. If the mutation also involves germ cells, offspring may inherit a constitutional NF1 mutation and develop generalised disease.
additionalDifferentials: Isolated multiple café-au-lait macules without neurofibromatosis
Becker naevus or other segmental pigmentary mosaicism
Piebaldism or naevus spilus with associated lesions
additionalInvestigations: Dermatological mapping of the segmental distribution and midline demarcation
Skin biopsy of a representative nodule for histological confirmation
Molecular testing for NF1 mutation on lesional tissue rather than peripheral blood
Ophthalmological review for Lisch nodules or optic pathway involvement
MRI of the affected region if deep plexiform or nerve involvement is suspected
Family assessment and genetic counselling for reproductive risk
redFlags: Rapid growth, new pain or neurological deficit in a lesion suggesting malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour
Extension beyond the original segment or emergence of generalised features
Unexplained skeletal deformity within the affected region
Visual disturbance suggesting optic pathway involvement
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is generally favourable with disease confined to the affected segment and a low rate of systemic complications, though there is a small lifelong risk of malignant transformation within neurofibromas and a rare reproductive risk of transmitting generalised NF1.
pitfalls: Testing peripheral blood for NF1 and reporting a false-negative result because the mutation is confined to lesional tissue.
Reassuring patients that offspring cannot be affected, overlooking possible gonadal mosaicism.
Mistaking segmental disease for benign isolated café-au-lait macules and omitting surveillance.
Failing to investigate a rapidly changing nodule for malignant transformation.
Assuming no systemic features can ever occur when deeper tissues may share the mutation.
references: Andrews' Diseases of the Skin: Clinical Dermatology
management: Manage conservatively with observation, as most disease is confined to the affected segment
Surgically excise neurofibromas that are symptomatic, disfiguring or functionally troublesome
Monitor lesions for malignant transformation such as rapid growth, pain or neurological deficit, prompting MRI and biopsy for a suspected malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour
Provide ophthalmological review, and regional MRI if deep plexiform or optic pathway involvement is suspected
Offer genetic counselling addressing the low reproductive risk of transmitting generalised NF1 through gonadal mosaicism
Provide dermatological follow-up with access to a neurofibromatosis specialist service
